questions.stem: Which description best fits the basic limited-liability characteristic taught for shareholders?

options.text: All shareholders must personally pay every corporate liability without limit
Shareholder exposure is generally limited by their investment or unpaid amount on shares, rather than every corporate debt automatically becoming a personal debt
Shareholders can never lose their investment
Company debts cease to exist when shares are issued

questions.explanation: Limited liability concerns shareholder exposure; it does not mean the business has no debts or risks.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6 — delivered material and governance slide summary

questions.stem: Which statement best reflects the lecture’s business-judgement discussion?

options.text: Every decision must maximise this week’s revenue
Directors are prohibited from considering any affected community
Good-faith managerial discretion can allow consideration of business context beyond immediate profit
Managers have unrestricted immunity for fraud

questions.explanation: The teaching examples challenge an absolute profit-only reading; discretion is not unlimited or a defence of fraud.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6 — delivered material and governance slide summary

questions.stem: How should the US corporate-purpose cases discussed in the lecture be used in an Irish-focused ethics question bank?

options.text: As guarantees that every manager will win any lawsuit
As teaching examples illustrating tensions, not as automatic statements of Irish law
As legislation that directly replaces all Irish company law
As proof that every corporation must ignore stakeholders

questions.explanation: The cases support conceptual discussion; jurisdiction-specific legal claims need separate verification.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6 — delivered material and governance slide summary

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the range of Workplace Relations Commission functions discussed in the lecture?

options.text: It includes advisory, inspection, mediation and adjudication functions
It offers mediation but has no adjudication function
It adjudicates disputes but has no inspection function
It deals only with employer complaints and not employee complaints

questions.explanation: The WRC has several functions, not just one dispute-resolution role.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6 — delivered material and governance slide summary

questions.stem: Which distinction matches the lecture’s Labour Court discussion?

options.text: Every Labour Court output is an identical non-binding suggestion
Every industrial-relations recommendation is automatically a criminal conviction
Industrial-relations recommendations and rights appeals have identical legal effects
Employment-rights appeal determinations and industrial-relations recommendations have different legal effects

questions.explanation: The lecture distinguishes binding employment-rights appeal determinations from non-binding industrial-relations recommendations.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6 — delivered material and governance slide summary

questions.stem: Which feature is central to recognising a potential protected disclosure in the lecture?

options.text: A reasonable belief in relevant wrongdoing encountered in a work-related context
Conclusive proof of every allegation before any report can be made
Any disagreement about personal taste unrelated to work
A personal financial interest in the reported outcome

questions.explanation: Reasonable belief and work-related wrongdoing are key; certainty of the final outcome is not required at the initial report stage.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6 — delivered material and governance slide summary

questions.stem: A worker reasonably believes a work practice is endangering safety and uses an appropriate reporting channel. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.text: It is automatically false if management disagrees
It may be a relevant wrongdoing report even before final investigation establishes every fact
It cannot be relevant unless an injury has already occurred
It can be relevant only if the worker personally suffered an injury

questions.explanation: The lecture includes safety risks and wrongdoing that may be occurring or likely to occur; the report is not a final finding.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6 — delivered material and governance slide summary

questions.stem: A complaint concerns only a personal interpersonal disagreement and alleges no relevant wrongdoing. Which route generally fits the distinction taught?

options.text: An ordinary grievance route rather than automatically treating it as a protected disclosure
Automatic classification as public-funds fraud
A requirement to report it to an unrelated regulator
Ignoring all workplace complaint procedures

questions.explanation: A purely interpersonal grievance is distinguished from relevant wrongdoing; mixed cases still need careful assessment.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6 — delivered material and governance slide summary

questions.stem: What should be checked before using an external prescribed reporting body?

options.text: Whether the reporter can publish every detail publicly first
Whether the body can guarantee a particular remedy in advance
Whether the alleged wrongdoing falls within that body’s remit
Whether the body is the most famous organisation available

questions.explanation: The appropriate external channel depends on the subject and remit, rather than choosing an arbitrary recipient.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6 — delivered material and governance slide summary

questions.stem: What does a prima facie assessment of a report establish?

options.text: A provisional initial basis for considering the case, not a final finding that wrongdoing is proved
An automatic final criminal conviction
That no investigation is needed
That confidentiality removes the need to assess the report

questions.explanation: The initial assessment is preliminary and must not be confused with a completed determination.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6 — delivered material and governance slide summary

questions.stem: Why distinguish a reasonably mistaken report from a knowingly false allegation?

options.text: Reasonable belief is not the same as deliberate fabrication
Every mistaken detail proves deliberate dishonesty
Only reports supported by a final court judgment can be made
A knowingly false allegation becomes reasonable whenever it is repeated

questions.explanation: The lecture emphasises the belief basis of a report; an error discovered later is not automatically knowing falsity.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6 — delivered material and governance slide summary

chapters.title: Foundations of Business Ethics
chapters.description: Ethical questions in business, law, judgement and the need for critical reasoning.

questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes law from ethics?

options.text: Law is enforceable by public institutions; ethics involves reasoned judgement about right conduct.
Law is personal preference; ethics is always criminal.
Law and ethics are identical.
Ethics applies only to private life.

questions.explanation: Law supplies formal rules and sanctions, while ethical evaluation can extend beyond them.

questions.stem: Why can technology create new ethical gaps?

options.text: Innovation may create harms before regulation catches up.
Technology makes every action transparent.
Technology prevents conflicts of interest.
New technology is automatically ethical.

questions.explanation: Rapid innovation can outpace lawmakers and expose issues not covered by existing rules.

questions.stem: Why does privatisation raise accountability questions?

options.text: Private organisations may deliver essential services while public accountability mechanisms are weaker.
Private firms cannot affect citizens.
Public services have no stakeholders.
Accountability concerns only profit.

questions.explanation: When essential functions move to firms, questions arise about transparency, responsibility and public interest.

questions.stem: What does critical ethical thinking require?

options.text: Examining reasons, evidence, stakeholders and consequences rather than relying on slogans
Choosing the first intuition only
Treating legality as the sole criterion
Ignoring uncertainty

questions.explanation: Ethical judgement should test assumptions and competing reasons.

questions.stem: What is the most defensible role for evidence in ethical judgement?

options.text: Values make evidence unnecessary.
Ethics begins by assuming allegations are true.
Evidence establishes relevant facts while frameworks evaluate what those facts require.
Facts alone mechanically produce one moral answer.

questions.explanation: Good reasoning separates factual claims from the ethical evaluation built on them.

chapters.title: Corporate Purpose & Responsibility
chapters.description: Friedman’s shareholder argument, corporate power and stakeholder consequences.

questions.stem: Which stakeholder is directly affected when a supplier cuts safety standards to meet a buyer’s price target?

options.text: Supply-chain workers
Only the buyer’s shareholders
No one outside the contract
Only tax authorities

questions.explanation: Commercial pressure can transfer risk to workers deeper in the supply chain.

questions.stem: What ethical tension is illustrated by very low retail prices linked to poor supply-chain conditions?

options.text: Consumer affordability versus responsibility for production impacts
Law versus mathematics
Technology versus language
Marketing versus accounting only

questions.explanation: Cheap goods can benefit consumers while hiding costs borne by vulnerable workers or communities.

questions.stem: Why might voluntary corporate responsibility be insufficient on its own?

options.text: Incentives can favour symbolic commitments over costly operational change.
Voluntary action is always illegal.
Firms never respond to reputation.
Stakeholders cannot observe conduct.

questions.explanation: Without oversight and aligned incentives, public commitments may not change underlying practices.

questions.stem: What is the strongest reason to examine corporate power ethically?

options.text: Business decisions can shape public choices and distribute risks beyond the firm.
Power guarantees good judgement.
Only governments affect society.
Corporate decisions concern owners alone.

questions.explanation: Scale and influence can create responsibilities beyond ordinary private transactions.

questions.stem: Which response best evaluates a profitable but harmful decision?

options.text: Consider profitability alongside duties, stakeholder harms and alternatives.
Accept it because profit settles every ethical question.
Reject it only if competitors complain.
Ignore people not named in the contract.

questions.explanation: Ethical analysis asks whether profit was achieved through acceptable treatment and consequences.

questions.stem: Which claim avoids oversimplifying the shareholder–stakeholder debate?

options.text: Profit is necessary for business, but its pursuit is constrained by rules and the effects imposed on others.
Profit and ethics can never coexist.
Any social initiative is automatically ethical.
Stakeholders always agree.

questions.explanation: A balanced analysis recognises commercial purpose while evaluating means, external effects and accountability.

questions.stem: Why can mixed motives still produce an ethical action?

options.text: Good intent guarantees good impact.
Motives never matter.
Commercial benefit does not erase genuine stakeholder benefit, though credibility needs evidence.
Any profit makes an action unethical.

questions.explanation: Ethical assessment can consider motives, methods and outcomes together.

questions.stem: What is purpose-washing?

options.text: Changing a legal structure.
Paying ordinary suppliers.
Promoting a social purpose that is not matched by core operations or accountability.
Publishing audited impact data.

questions.explanation: A purpose claim is weak when practice and incentives contradict it.

questions.stem: Which question best tests corporate responsibility for a supplier?

options.text: Did the buyer avoid direct employment?
Was the product popular?
What influence, knowledge and foreseeable effects did the buyer have?
Is the supplier in another country?

questions.explanation: Responsibility depends on power, knowledge and effects, not only formal ownership.

questions.stem: Why can limited liability strengthen the case for social duties?

options.text: Society grants owners protection from some losses, raising reciprocal questions about corporate impacts.
It makes shareholders liable without limit.
It removes corporate legal identity.
It guarantees philanthropy.

questions.explanation: The legal privilege can be paired with expectations of responsible conduct.

chapters.title: Authority, Roles & Situational Pressure
chapters.description: Stanford prison and Milgram studies, obedience, roles and situational explanations.

questions.stem: What broad question did the Stanford prison study appear to investigate?

options.text: How assigned social roles and institutional settings influence behaviour
How prices reach equilibrium
How databases store records
How exercise affects memory

questions.explanation: The study examined behaviour in a simulated prison environment.

questions.stem: What later criticism weakens the claim that Stanford guards became cruel spontaneously?

options.text: Guards received orientation and some were encouraged to adopt particular roles.
No participants were assigned roles.
The study used no prison setting.
Every participant refused to continue immediately.

questions.explanation: Coaching and demand characteristics make it harder to attribute behaviour purely to the situation.

questions.stem: What is a demand characteristic?

options.text: A cue that leads participants to behave as they think the study expects
A market shortage
A legal duty to publish results
A personality disorder

questions.explanation: Participants may perform an expected role rather than reveal natural behaviour.

questions.stem: What lesson can still be drawn cautiously from the Stanford study?

options.text: Authority can frame harmful conduct as serving a legitimate or greater purpose.
Every person becomes sadistic in a uniform.
Situations never influence conduct.
The study proves one universal personality type.

questions.explanation: Even with methodological flaws, role expectations and legitimising narratives can influence conduct.

questions.stem: In Milgram’s classic setup, what role did participants believe they had?

options.text: Teacher administering shocks for incorrect answers
Prison guard
Corporate auditor
Election observer

questions.explanation: Participants were assigned the teacher role while the learner was part of the experimental setup.

questions.stem: What proportion reached the maximum shock level in the classic Milgram condition discussed?

options.text: About 65%
About 5%
Exactly 100%
No one

questions.explanation: The lecture reported that 65% continued to the maximum labelled level.

questions.stem: What is the agentic state explanation of obedience?

options.text: A person sees themselves as carrying out an authority’s wishes and shifts responsibility upward.
A person becomes financially independent.
A group reaches unanimous agreement.
A participant forgets the instructions.

questions.explanation: Perceived agency and responsibility move toward the authority figure.

questions.stem: Which change tended to reduce obedience in Milgram-style variations?

options.text: Peers openly resisting the authority
Increasing the authority’s proximity
Increasing institutional prestige
Making escalation gradual

questions.explanation: Social support for resistance makes disobedience more psychologically available.

questions.stem: Why can gradual escalation increase compliance?

options.text: Each small step makes the next step easier to rationalise and creates commitment.
It makes the authority disappear.
It removes every consequence.
It turns orders into laws.

questions.explanation: Incremental increases can bind a person to previous choices before the full severity is apparent.

questions.stem: Which is a valid ethical criticism of Milgram’s study?

options.text: Participants experienced deception and significant distress, raising consent and withdrawal concerns.
The study had no human participants.
It revealed participants’ real names publicly in class.
It measured only market prices.

questions.explanation: The design placed participants under pressure while concealing the study’s true purpose.

questions.stem: In Milgram’s study, what did the learner’s protests test?

options.text: Whether memory improves with real shocks.
Whether teachers knew the learner personally.
Whether the machine measured intelligence.
Whether participants would continue under authority despite apparent harm.

questions.explanation: The conflict between obedience and concern for the learner was central.

questions.stem: Why does experimenter distance tend to reduce obedience?

options.text: The authority becomes less immediate and easier to resist.
The learner becomes invisible.
The shocks become real.
Peers become more obedient automatically.

questions.explanation: Proximity affects the authority’s social pressure.

questions.stem: Why is “I was following orders” not a complete moral defence?

options.text: Authorities always possess better ethics.
Responsibility belongs only to victims.
Situational pressure helps explain conduct but does not automatically remove agency or responsibility.
Orders make every act lawful.

questions.explanation: Explanation and excuse are separate questions.

questions.stem: What is the safest conclusion from the Stanford prison evidence?

options.text: The study had no demand characteristics.
Role expectations and researcher cues can influence behaviour, but the classic spontaneous-sadism claim is overstated.
Any assigned guard becomes cruel.
The study proves personality never matters.

questions.explanation: Coaching and performance weaken the strongest original claim.

questions.stem: Why are later obedience studies not directly percentage-comparable with Milgram’s classic condition?

options.text: Methods, safeguards, samples and stopping rules differ.
Percentages cannot describe behaviour.
Modern participants never face authority.
Milgram used no experimental design.

questions.explanation: Design differences limit simple numerical comparison.

chapters.title: Bias, Rationalisation & Leadership
chapters.description: Cognitive biases and psychological mechanisms that shape ethical judgement.

questions.stem: How does an amoral manager differ from an immoral manager?

options.text: An amoral manager shows little concern for moral considerations; an immoral manager knowingly acts against them.
They are identical by definition.
An amoral manager always follows every duty.
An immoral manager is unaware of consequences.

questions.explanation: The distinction concerns indifference to ethics versus conscious wrongdoing.

questions.stem: A board interprets ambiguous evidence as confirming its existing strategy. Which bias fits best?

options.text: Limited liability
Act utilitarianism
Externality
Biased assimilation

questions.explanation: Prior commitments shape how mixed evidence is evaluated.

questions.stem: What is the best organisational response to overconfidence?

options.text: Reward certainty and suppress dissent.
Remove all data.
Let the most senior view prevail.
Independent challenge, decision records and tests against disconfirming evidence.

questions.explanation: Structured challenge reduces reliance on confidence as evidence.

chapters.title: Ethical Culture, Incentives & Organisational Systems
chapters.description: How language, incentives, distance, governance and leadership shape conduct.

questions.stem: How can reward systems undermine ethical conduct?

options.text: They can make short-term targets more salient than duties or stakeholder harm.
Rewards eliminate self-interest.
Bonuses automatically improve oversight.
Targets cannot influence behaviour.

questions.explanation: People respond to what the organisation measures and rewards.

questions.stem: Which control best addresses pressure to manipulate sales figures?

options.text: Combine realistic targets with independent checks, speak-up channels and consequences for misreporting.
Raise targets and remove audits.
Reward results regardless of method.
Keep reporting rules ambiguous.

questions.explanation: Aligned incentives and oversight reduce both pressure and opportunity for misconduct.

questions.stem: Why is an ethics code alone often insufficient?

options.text: Actual incentives, leadership behaviour and enforcement may contradict the document.
Written rules cannot be read.
Codes are always illegal.
Employees never notice leaders.

questions.explanation: Culture is produced by practice and accountability, not merely formal statements.

questions.stem: What is “tone at the top”?

options.text: The example and priorities communicated by senior leaders
The volume of a manager’s voice
A public advertising slogan only
A legal definition of profit

questions.explanation: Employees infer acceptable conduct from what leaders do, reward and tolerate.

questions.stem: Which organisational feature helps counter conformity?

options.text: Protected channels for challenge and leaders who invite dissent
Punishing all disagreement
Keeping decisions secret
Rewarding only unanimity

questions.explanation: Psychological safety and protected escalation make concerns easier to raise.

questions.stem: What makes an ethical programme credible?

options.text: Consistent leadership, aligned incentives, training, reporting routes, investigation and accountability
A slogan with no operational change
A single annual email
Profit growth alone

questions.explanation: Credibility requires systems that reinforce stated values in everyday decisions.

questions.stem: What does psychological safety support?

options.text: Secrecy around failures.
Removal of accountability.
Raising concerns and admitting mistakes without disproportionate retaliation.
Guaranteed agreement with leaders.

questions.explanation: People are more likely to surface risk when challenge is safe.

questions.stem: Why should an ethics hotline be independent and protected?

options.text: Anonymous concerns are always true.
Employees may otherwise fear retaliation or suppression by implicated managers.
Independence removes the need to investigate.
Only customers can report concerns.

questions.explanation: Protected channels improve access while allegations still require fair investigation.

questions.stem: What is incentive compatibility in an ethics programme?

options.text: Targets and rewards support rather than undermine stated standards.
Every employee receives the same pay.
Rules are hidden from staff.
Profit is never measured.

questions.explanation: Conduct follows what organisations reward as well as what they say.

questions.stem: Which metric best tests whether an ethics programme works?

options.text: The chief executive’s speech count.
Patterns in reporting, investigation, retaliation, outcomes and repeated misconduct.
The number of posters printed.
The length of the code alone.

questions.explanation: Operational evidence is more informative than symbolic activity.

questions.stem: What is diffusion of responsibility?

options.text: One leader accepts every consequence.
A firm discloses its supply chain.
A whistleblower documents a concern.
Accountability weakens because each participant assumes someone else owns the issue.

questions.explanation: Fragmented roles can allow foreseeable harms to fall between functions.

chapters.title: Externalities, Global Business & Evidence
chapters.description: Stakeholder impacts, externalised costs, global supply chains and evidence-based ethical claims.

questions.stem: What is a negative externality?

options.text: A cost imposed on people outside the market transaction
A discount received by a buyer
A cost recorded fully in the seller’s accounts
A voluntary donation

questions.explanation: Externalities occur when some consequences fall on third parties and are omitted from the private exchange.

questions.stem: Why are externalities ethically important?

options.text: People may bear harms without choosing or benefiting from the transaction.
They always increase profit.
They affect only accountants.
They are included automatically in every price.

questions.explanation: Consent, fairness and responsibility become concerns when costs are shifted to outsiders.

questions.stem: Why should claims about fast-fashion harm be made carefully?

options.text: Specific allegations require reliable evidence rather than assumption or viral repetition.
Fast fashion has no ethical issues.
Evidence is irrelevant to ethics.
Only prices may be discussed.

questions.explanation: Ethical criticism is stronger when it distinguishes documented facts from general suspicion.

questions.stem: How can a company externalise environmental costs?

options.text: By leaving pollution or resource depletion for communities and future generations to bear
By paying all clean-up costs itself
By reducing harmful emissions
By disclosing verified impacts

questions.explanation: Externalisation shifts costs away from the firm and transaction.

questions.stem: What is “woke-washing” in the covered material?

options.text: Publicly signalling progressive values without matching operational practice
Changing every company logo
Publishing audited evidence of improvement
Ending all marketing

questions.explanation: The criticism concerns a gap between values-based messaging and actual conduct.

questions.stem: Which evidence would best test whether a values-based campaign is substantive?

options.text: Operational targets, resource allocation, verified outcomes and accountability
The campaign slogan alone
Celebrity approval only
The number of social-media likes

questions.explanation: Substance appears in changed decisions and measurable, scrutinised results.

questions.stem: What did the facial-scar perception example illustrate?

options.text: Expectations can shape how people interpret ambiguous social treatment.
Visible scars determine every interaction.
Perception always matches objective treatment.
Experiments cannot use deception.

questions.explanation: Participants’ expectations influenced their interpretation even when the apparent scar had been removed.

questions.stem: What is the best method for evaluating a dramatic corporate-ethics claim?

options.text: Identify the claim, check credible evidence, consider alternative explanations and separate fact from inference.
Share it immediately if it confirms prior beliefs.
Assume legality proves morality.
Ignore who is affected.

questions.explanation: Evidence-based ethical analysis guards against biased assimilation and unsupported accusation.

questions.stem: A product’s low price excludes pollution costs borne by residents. What is this?

options.text: Consumer surplus only
A positive right
A sunk cost
A negative externality

questions.explanation: Part of the social cost is shifted outside the transaction.

questions.stem: Why is a vivid photograph insufficient proof of a general business claim?

options.text: Images cannot contain information.
Only numerical evidence is ethical.
One example proves every case.
It may illustrate harm without establishing prevalence, causation or representativeness.

questions.explanation: Evidence quality depends on how well it supports the scope of the claim.

questions.stem: What does due diligence require in a high-risk supply chain?

options.text: Assume distance removes responsibility.
Identify, prevent, mitigate and account for foreseeable harms.
Rely solely on a supplier promise.
Stop collecting evidence.

questions.explanation: Due diligence is an ongoing risk-management and accountability process.

questions.stem: Why may consumers struggle to discipline harmful supply chains?

options.text: Consumers have perfect traceability.
Every ethical product is cheaper.
Firms cannot change suppliers.
Information is incomplete and individual purchasing power is limited.

questions.explanation: Information and collective-action problems constrain consumer choice.

questions.stem: Which statement best avoids an ethical overclaim?

options.text: The evidence indicates a risk requiring investigation, but does not yet prove every actor caused the harm.
The allegation proves guilt.
No documented harm can ever occur.
Profit establishes innocence.

questions.explanation: Calibrated claims preserve uncertainty while taking credible risks seriously.

chapters.title: Consequences, Context & Utilitarianism
chapters.description: Consequentialism, relativism, Bentham, Mill and cost–benefit reasoning.

questions.stem: What does moral relativism claim?

options.text: Law and ethics are identical.
Standards are shaped by cultural context.
One objective rule is obvious everywhere.
Consequences never matter.

questions.explanation: Relativism emphasises the cultural formation of moral judgement.

questions.stem: A safety measure costs €1 million and prevents widespread serious harm. What must utilitarian analysis include?

options.text: All significant stakeholder benefits and costs, not profit alone.
Only the firm’s cash outlay.
Only majority preferences.
Only legal penalties.

questions.explanation: Welfare analysis counts external and long-term consequences.

questions.stem: In the trolley problem, what feature creates the classic utilitarian appeal?

options.text: Duties are legally defined.
The outcome is unknowable by design.
Sacrificing one appears to save a larger number.
No one is harmed.

questions.explanation: The case tests whether aggregate welfare justifies imposing a severe cost on one.

chapters.title: Duties, Character, Rights & Justice
chapters.description: Kant, virtue ethics, rights, Rawls, discourse ethics and pluralism.

questions.stem: How does Rawls differ from utilitarianism?

options.text: Rawls ignores fairness.
Rawls treats profit as the only good.
There is no difference.
Rawls protects basic liberties and the least advantaged rather than simply maximising the total.

questions.explanation: Justice as fairness constrains aggregate maximisation.

questions.stem: What does ethical pluralism recommend?

options.text: Treat every answer as equally valid.
Abandon principles.
Choose the most profitable theory.
Use multiple relevant frameworks and seek justified overlap rather than one automatic test.

questions.explanation: Different frameworks expose different moral features of a dilemma.

chapters.title: Stakeholders, Governance & CSR
chapters.description: Stakeholder classifications, corporate governance and CSR credibility.

questions.stem: Who is a stakeholder?

options.text: Only an owner of shares.
Only a government regulator.
Only a paying customer.
A person or group that affects or is affected by the organisation.

questions.explanation: Stakeholding is broader than equity ownership.

questions.stem: Which order matches Carroll’s CSR pyramid from base upward?

options.text: Legal, economic, philanthropic, ethical.
Ethical, economic, legal, philanthropic.
Economic, legal, ethical, philanthropic.
Philanthropic, ethical, legal, economic.

questions.explanation: Carroll places economic responsibility at the foundation, followed by legal, ethical and philanthropic.

questions.stem: Why should Dodge v Ford be read cautiously?

options.text: It concerns no corporation.
It prohibits managerial judgement.
A historical case does not prove a universal duty to maximise short-term profit at any cost.
It abolished shareholder interests.

questions.explanation: Later doctrine and context complicate the simplified shareholder-primacy slogan.

questions.stem: What is credible CSR most likely to show?

options.text: Governance, resources and measurable operational change aligned with the claim.
A donation unrelated to core harm.
A campaign with no targets.
Legal compliance presented as exceptional generosity.

questions.explanation: Credibility depends on what the business changes and can account for.

questions.stem: Why can philanthropy fail to offset harmful core operations?

options.text: Philanthropy is always illegal.
The scale and source of harm may outweigh a separate charitable benefit.
Donations erase causation.
Stakeholders consider only intent.

questions.explanation: CSR must be assessed against the whole business model.

chapters.title: Consumerism, GDP & Wellbeing
chapters.description: Consumer identity, GDP limits, wellbeing measures and degrowth.

questions.stem: What is consumerism in the lecture?

options.text: Any act of buying necessities.
A ban on advertising.
A national accounting measure.
A pattern linking identity and wellbeing strongly to acquiring goods and services.

questions.explanation: Consumerism concerns social meaning and continual acquisition, not purchase alone.

questions.stem: Why is GDP an incomplete wellbeing measure?

options.text: It excludes all market activity.
It is identical to household income.
It records output but omits many distributional, social and environmental conditions.
It measures happiness perfectly.

questions.explanation: Output can rise alongside inequality, insecurity or environmental damage.

questions.stem: What benefit of GDP growth should a balanced critique retain?

options.text: Growth never affects life expectancy.
Only symbolic consumption changes.
GDP automatically ensures equality.
Growth has supported major improvements in material living standards and health.

questions.explanation: GDP is useful even though it is not sufficient.

questions.stem: What is symbolic consumption?

options.text: Reducing product variety.
Buying partly to express identity, status or belonging.
Purchasing only basic food.
Measuring public output.

questions.explanation: Products can carry social meaning beyond practical function.

questions.stem: What are the three elements of the triple bottom line?

options.text: People, planet and profit.
Price, promotion and place.
Law, ethics and morals.
Income, inflation and interest.

questions.explanation: The framework broadens performance beyond finance.

questions.stem: What does Gross National Happiness challenge?

options.text: The assumption that GDP growth alone represents national progress.
The value of social support.
The use of public policy.
The existence of environmental limits.

questions.explanation: It treats happiness, equity and sustainability as policy goals.

questions.stem: Which is one of Pretty et al.’s wellbeing pathways?

options.text: Longer commuting time.
Family and community connections.
Maximum advertising exposure.
Higher product turnover.

questions.explanation: Social connection is one of six pathways alongside food, activity, mind, nature and meaningful possessions.

questions.stem: How does degrowth differ from recession?

options.text: Degrowth requires greater waste.
Recession guarantees justice.
Degrowth is a planned reorganisation toward lower resource use and wellbeing; recession is an unplanned contraction.
They are identical.

questions.explanation: Degrowth is a normative transformation, not simply falling GDP.

questions.stem: Why can apparent brand variety be misleading?

options.text: Every brand is legally independent.
Ownership never affects choice.
Labels disclose all supply chains.
Many brands may share common owners and concentrated decision power.

questions.explanation: Market concentration can reduce meaningful diversity behind the shelf.

questions.stem: What ethical issue do warning labels raise?

options.text: Whether information is always manipulation.
Whether health has no social cost.
Whether consumers lack all agency.
How to support informed autonomy without ignoring industry design and vulnerable consumers.

questions.explanation: The issue balances information, freedom, risk and responsibility.

chapters.title: Bottom of the Pyramid, Fairtrade & Microfinance
chapters.description: Low-income markets, appropriate innovation, trade, aid and finance.

questions.stem: Who are the Bottom of the Pyramid in this context?

options.text: Government employees.
Corporate shareholders.
Large populations living on very low incomes and often underserved by mainstream business.
Only wealthy early adopters.

questions.explanation: BOP refers to low-income consumers and producers excluded from conventional markets.

questions.stem: What is the poverty penalty?

options.text: A reward for saving.
A subsidy to large firms.
Poor consumers may pay more per unit or face worse terms because of limited access and scale.
A tax charged only on profit.

questions.explanation: Small purchases, weak infrastructure and lack of credit can raise effective costs.

questions.stem: Why is a smaller package not automatically good BOP innovation?

options.text: Affordability guarantees value.
Packaging has no stakeholder effect.
It may improve access while charging a higher unit price and creating more waste.
Small packs always reduce waste.

questions.explanation: Ethical assessment includes unit cost, usefulness and externalities.

questions.stem: What does co-creation add to BOP design?

options.text: Removal of customer feedback.
Guaranteed profit.
Local knowledge and participation in defining useful solutions.
A foreign design imposed unchanged.

questions.explanation: Local participation reduces the risk of unsuitable products.

questions.stem: What is Project Shakti?

options.text: A tobacco settlement.
A climate treaty.
A social-media algorithm.
A model training and financing rural women to distribute products in India.

questions.explanation: It combines livelihood opportunities with hard-to-reach distribution.

questions.stem: What is a central ethical question about microfinance?

options.text: Whether repayment is always harmful.
Whether access to credit creates durable empowerment or burdens vulnerable borrowers with debt.
Whether loans contain any numbers.
Whether banks can use money.

questions.explanation: Repayment rates alone do not establish positive welfare impact.

questions.stem: Why can Fairtrade be criticised despite good intentions?

options.text: Certification may not build enough producer capability or local value capture.
Trade can never help development.
Every certified product is fraudulent.
Producers do not need income.

questions.explanation: Critics ask who captures value and whether the model changes structural dependence.

questions.stem: What is cultural pollution in BOP debates?

options.text: Marketing and products may displace local practices and impose outside aspirations.
A measurable air pollutant only.
Any cultural exchange.
Local product design.

questions.explanation: Commercial influence can alter values and practices as well as consumption.

questions.stem: What is the strongest critique of simple one-for-one aid models?

options.text: Local markets do not exist.
Recipients always reject goods.
They may create dependence or disrupt local producers without solving structural causes.
Donations never provide benefit.

questions.explanation: Impact depends on systems and unintended effects, not the donation count alone.

questions.stem: Why should microfinance evaluation look beyond repayment?

options.text: Positive impact requires default.
Borrowers may repay through hardship, refinancing or sacrifice without improved wellbeing.
Repayment data are never real.
Only lenders are stakeholders.

questions.explanation: Financial performance is not identical to social outcome.

chapters.title: Tobacco, Pharma & OxyContin
chapters.description: Addiction, information asymmetry, marketing and distributed accountability.

questions.stem: Why does addiction complicate the consumer-choice defence?

options.text: Consumers lose every form of agency.
Repeated purchase may not reflect fully free and informed choice.
Addiction increases information symmetry.
Harm becomes irrelevant when a product is legal.

questions.explanation: Dependence can weaken autonomy without removing all personal responsibility.

questions.stem: What is information asymmetry in the tobacco or opioid cases?

options.text: Only regulators know product prices.
Advertising removes uncertainty.
Firms may know more about risks than consumers, patients or prescribers.
Everyone has identical evidence.

questions.explanation: Unequal knowledge can undermine informed consent.

questions.stem: Why are price discounts a form of tobacco promotion?

options.text: They eliminate segmentation.
They lower effective prices and can encourage purchase even without a conventional advert.
They increase every health warning.
They prohibit retailer sales.

questions.explanation: Marketing includes pricing and distribution incentives.

questions.stem: What ethical problem arises from targeting communities already facing disadvantage?

options.text: Marketing may exploit vulnerability and concentrate harm.
Segmentation is always neutral.
Only shareholders are affected.
Legal products have no externalities.

questions.explanation: Unequal exposure matters to justice and stakeholder analysis.

questions.stem: What is a public-health externality of addictive products?

options.text: Treatment and family costs fall partly on people outside the sale.
The buyer pays a listed price.
The firm records revenue.
A shareholder receives a dividend.

questions.explanation: Private transactions can transfer costs to health systems and communities.

questions.stem: Why does the OxyContin case broaden responsibility beyond Purdue?

options.text: Only the final consumer acts.
Legal settlements remove causation.
Supply chains cannot share responsibility.
Consultants, distributors, prescribers and regulators may contribute to cumulative harm.

questions.explanation: Complex harm can arise from interacting decisions across a system.

questions.stem: What governance failure can aggressive sales incentives create?

options.text: Employees may minimise risk information to meet targets.
Targets guarantee accurate disclosure.
Bonuses eliminate conflicts of interest.
Sales teams set public-health law.

questions.explanation: Incentives can reward volume while weakening risk control.

questions.stem: Does a settlement alone establish moral accountability?

options.text: Yes; money proves sincere remorse.
Yes; courts decide every ethical question.
No; settlements are never relevant.
No; payment can resolve claims while responsibility is still denied or contested.

questions.explanation: Legal resolution and moral acknowledgement are related but distinct.

questions.stem: How would Kantian ethics assess deceptive risk marketing?

options.text: It asks only whether competitors do it.
It uses patients as means by undermining informed agency.
It is acceptable whenever profitable.
It counts only aggregate pleasure.

questions.explanation: Respect for persons requires truthful information and non-manipulation.

questions.stem: What is the strongest utilitarian test of an addictive product strategy?

options.text: Count company revenue only.
Assume every purchase adds welfare.
Ignore indirect consequences.
Compare total benefits with health, family and social harms over time.

questions.explanation: Utilitarianism requires the full balance of stakeholder outcomes.

chapters.title: Ultra-Processed Food & Market Power
chapters.description: Food formulation, evidence, concentration, autonomy and responsibility.

questions.stem: What distinguishes ultra-processed food from ordinary processed food?

options.text: Any cooked food is ultra-processed.
Processing means adding water only.
UPFs contain one recognisable ingredient.
UPFs are industrial formulations using multiple ingredients and processes for convenience, shelf life and palatability.

questions.explanation: The category concerns formulation and industrial processing, not any alteration.

questions.stem: Why does an association between UPF intake and disease not by itself prove causation?

options.text: Health outcomes cannot be measured.
Other factors and study design may explain part of the relationship.
Associations contain no evidence.
Causation requires a company admission.

questions.explanation: Observational evidence needs careful interpretation and corroboration.

questions.stem: What is the cautious conclusion from food–drug reward similarities?

options.text: Reward mechanisms may overlap, but similarity does not prove identical addiction.
Sugar and cocaine are ethically identical.
Food has no reward effect.
Every consumer becomes dependent.

questions.explanation: Analogy can guide questions without settling degree or causality.

questions.stem: How can market concentration reduce meaningful consumer choice?

options.text: Retailers cannot influence choice.
A few firms may control formulation, prices, distribution and shelf access.
More brands always mean more owners.
Concentration removes bargaining power from large firms.

questions.explanation: Visible variety may mask concentrated control.

questions.stem: Why are farmers stakeholders in food-market concentration?

options.text: Farmers buy no food.
Only consumers face bargaining power.
Concentration guarantees higher farm income.
Dominant buyers can shape terms, prices and market access.

questions.explanation: Power can be exercised upstream as well as toward consumers.

questions.stem: What autonomy concern arises from engineered palatability?

options.text: Design may exploit predictable cues to increase consumption beyond reflective choice.
Taste eliminates all responsibility.
Pleasure is always unethical.
Formulation cannot influence behaviour.

questions.explanation: The concern is intentional use of superior behavioural knowledge.

questions.stem: How can GLP-1 medicines create a food–pharma incentive conflict?

options.text: Treatment and prevention always align.
One sector may profit from treating conditions partly linked to another sector’s products.
Medicines remove every prevention need.
Food firms sell no health-related products.

questions.explanation: Commercial systems may reward treatment without correcting causes.

questions.stem: Why is reformulation not necessarily business-model change?

options.text: Reformulation removes market power.
Health labels prevent overconsumption.
A healthier product can coexist with aggressive volume growth and marketing.
Any ingredient change ends externalities.

questions.explanation: Impact depends on total operations and consumption, not one product metric.

questions.stem: What evidence would strengthen a causal UPF claim?

options.text: A single dramatic headline.
One brand advertisement.
A correlation with no controls.
Converging results from appropriate longitudinal, experimental and mechanistic research.

questions.explanation: Multiple methods can address confounding and mechanisms.

questions.stem: What is shared responsibility in this context?

options.text: Only consumers matter.
Only manufacturers matter.
Responsibility must be equal among all actors.
Consumers retain agency while firms, retailers and regulators also shape choices and risks.

questions.explanation: Responsibility can be distributed unequally according to power and knowledge.

chapters.title: AI, Social Media & Data Ethics
chapters.description: AI reliability, concentration, labour, profiling and platform responsibility.

questions.stem: What is an AI hallucination?

options.text: A legal ownership form.
A guaranteed prediction.
A confident output that is unsupported or false.
A verified training record.

questions.explanation: Generative systems can produce plausible language without factual grounding.

questions.stem: Why are hallucinations especially concerning in high-stakes use?

options.text: Errors become harmless at scale.
Confidence proves accuracy.
Users may rely on false outputs in decisions affecting rights, safety or health.
High-stakes users need no evidence.

questions.explanation: Consequences magnify the need for validation and oversight.

questions.stem: What economic risk can AI investment concentration create?

options.text: Valuation proves social benefit.
Technology firms cannot fail.
A reversal in expectations can affect markets and exposed economies.
Concentration guarantees stable returns.

questions.explanation: Systemic exposure matters beyond model behaviour.

questions.stem: What labour tension accompanies AI productivity claims?

options.text: Productivity and labour are unrelated.
Only investors are stakeholders.
Gains may depend partly on replacing work, affecting employment and income distribution.
Automation always raises every wage.

questions.explanation: Efficiency benefits can be distributed unevenly.

questions.stem: How did Cambridge Analytica-style profiling create ethical risk?

options.text: Targeting was visible to everyone.
Only public census data were used.
Seemingly trivial data enabled sensitive inference and political microtargeting.
The data could not predict traits.

questions.explanation: Low-friction data can support opaque persuasion.

questions.stem: When can personalisation become manipulation?

options.text: Only when users pay money.
When a recommendation is accurate.
When hidden profiling exploits vulnerabilities to steer choices against informed interests.
Whenever content is relevant.

questions.explanation: Transparency, autonomy and power distinguish assistance from exploitation.

questions.stem: Why can a platform bear responsibility for user-generated content?

options.text: Hosting removes all causal influence.
Algorithms are neutral by definition.
Users cannot be stakeholders.
Its ranking and recommendation systems shape reach, incentives and foreseeable harm.

questions.explanation: Design choices mediate what receives attention.

questions.stem: What is an addictive-design conflict of interest?

options.text: Design cannot affect habits.
Revenue rises with engagement even when compulsive use harms users.
Users and platforms always want identical outcomes.
Attention has no commercial value.

questions.explanation: The business model can reward behaviour contrary to wellbeing.

questions.stem: Why are children treated as especially vulnerable online?

options.text: Advertising cannot reach minors.
Their judgement and resistance to persuasive design are still developing.
Children never use platforms.
Age has no relationship to consent.

questions.explanation: Developmental vulnerability can justify stronger duties and safeguards.

questions.stem: Which governance response best fits high-risk AI deployment?

options.text: Hide known limitations.
Independent evaluation, monitoring, human accountability and limits proportionate to harm.
Rely on the developer’s confidence only.
Deploy everywhere before testing.

questions.explanation: Risk governance needs evidence, control and clear responsibility.

chapters.title: Sustainability, Plastics & Corporate Credibility
chapters.description: Climate justice, circularity, SDGs, plastics and B Corps.

questions.stem: What is environmental justice?

options.text: Treating climate effects as identical everywhere.
Counting emissions without people.
Fair distribution of environmental benefits, harms and decision power.
Maximising recycling labels.

questions.explanation: Communities contributing least may bear the greatest consequences.

questions.stem: What does a circular economy aim to do?

options.text: Increase disposal after one use.
Rely only on landfill taxes.
Maximise virgin-material extraction.
Design out waste and keep products and materials in use.

questions.explanation: Circular design prioritises prevention, durability, reuse and recovery.

questions.stem: Why is prevention generally preferred to recycling alone?

options.text: Avoiding waste and virgin production addresses impacts before disposal.
Recycling always uses no energy.
Every recyclable item is recycled.
Prevention eliminates product use.

questions.explanation: End-of-pipe recycling cannot fully offset growing material throughput.

questions.stem: Why can “recyclable” be a misleading comfort?

options.text: Recyclable products are never collected.
The label proves circularity.
Recycling has no infrastructure needs.
Technical recyclability does not mean collection and actual recycling occur.

questions.explanation: Real outcomes depend on systems, economics and behaviour.

questions.stem: What greenwashing risk appears in a clean-up alliance formed by major plastic producers?

options.text: Clean-up always changes the core model.
Alliance membership proves impact.
Production volume is irrelevant.
Visible removal may be tiny compared with continued growth in virgin plastic output.

questions.explanation: Credibility requires comparing the initiative with the scale of core operations.

questions.stem: What is procedural climate justice?

options.text: The richest actor decides alone.
Only total emissions matter.
Lobbying power is ethically neutral.
Affected and vulnerable groups have meaningful influence over decisions.

questions.explanation: Fair process concerns who participates and whose interests shape agreements.

questions.stem: How should the SDGs be understood for this module?

options.text: A climate treaty limited to emissions.
An interconnected framework for social, economic and environmental progress.
A requirement to memorise every target only.
A corporate certification.

questions.explanation: The lecture emphasises concepts and connections.

questions.stem: What is a B Corp?

options.text: A company certified by B Lab against impact and governance standards.
Any company making a donation.
A universal legal form.
A government agency.

questions.explanation: Certification is a private standard with assessment and transparency requirements.

questions.stem: How does a benefit corporation differ from B Corp certification?

options.text: It requires no stakeholder purpose.
It is a legal corporate form available in some jurisdictions.
It is the same B Lab award.
It means tax-exempt charity.

questions.explanation: Legal status and private certification can overlap but are distinct.

questions.stem: What would best demonstrate credible sustainability strategy?

options.text: Counting only waste collected.
Lifecycle targets, governance, investment and verified reductions aligned with core production.
A slogan without baseline data.
One sponsored event.

questions.explanation: Credibility requires measurable change across the business model.

chapters.title: Discussion Group 1: Low-Cost Clothing
chapters.description: Child labour, sourcing incentives and responsible transition.

questions.stem: What is the buyer’s central conflict in the case?

options.text: Meeting price and career targets versus foreseeable worker harm.
Choosing a web framework.
Setting an interest rate.
Reducing carbon through recycling.

questions.explanation: Commercial incentives collide with duties to vulnerable supply-chain workers.

questions.stem: Why may an immediate supplier boycott harm families?

options.text: Income can be essential where alternatives and social protection are weak.
Child labour has no costs.
Every supplier is identical.
Education is already guaranteed.

questions.explanation: Removing work without transition support can worsen short-term survival.

questions.stem: Why is that risk not a justification for the status quo?

options.text: Local norms settle ethics.
Low prices prove consent.
Limited alternatives should not excuse unsafe work, lost education or bribery.
Poverty eliminates rights.

questions.explanation: Context shapes remedies but does not erase minimum protections.

questions.stem: What does bribing an inspector show?

options.text: Monitoring is unnecessary.
Corruption benefits every stakeholder.
Even the claim of legal compliance is doubtful.
The supplier exceeds governance standards.

questions.explanation: Bribery undermines enforcement and the legality defence.

questions.stem: How would Kant assess the use of child labour for cheap garments?

options.text: Children are treated merely as means to price and promotion goals.
It is acceptable if total sales rise.
It is ethical if common locally.
Only contract law matters.

questions.explanation: The humanity formulation protects persons from instrumental exploitation.

questions.stem: What would Rawls ask in this case?

options.text: How many garments sell?
Would the sourcing rules be accepted without knowing whether one is child, parent, buyer or shareholder?
Which option maximises buyer promotion?
What local practice is most common?

questions.explanation: The veil of ignorance tests impartial fairness.

questions.stem: What is the strongest responsible-sourcing response?

options.text: Investigate, reject bribery and fund monitored improvements with a credible transition.
Ignore household income.
Move quietly to an equally risky supplier.
Accept certification without verification.

questions.explanation: Remediation should reduce harm without abandoning workers.

questions.stem: Why does ethical certification not end the retailer’s responsibility?

options.text: Certificates make evidence unnecessary.
Agents own all retailer decisions.
Certification transfers legal identity.
The retailer must assess actual conditions and the reliability of assurance.

questions.explanation: Formal assurance can fail or mask subcontracting.

questions.stem: What does stakeholder mapping reveal?

options.text: Only consumers benefit.
The buyer has no agency.
Those bearing the greatest risk often have the least power over price and contracts.
Every stakeholder has equal influence.

questions.explanation: Power and exposure are unevenly distributed.

questions.stem: What would discourse ethics add?

options.text: The retailer should decide secretly.
Local voices have no relevance.
Dialogue replaces evidence.
Affected families and workers should participate in designing the remedy.

questions.explanation: Legitimacy improves when those affected can shape the solution.

questions.stem: In the discussion group’s micro/meso/macro framework, investigating a supplier factory’s management practices and worker records is primarily which level?

options.text: Macro: national legislation and institutions.
Macro: any action involving more than one worker.
Micro: the company or factory.
Meso: the surrounding town’s alternative livelihoods.

questions.explanation: As used in this discussion, micro concerns company/factory decisions; meso concerns the community; macro concerns wider law and sociocultural conditions.
questions.source: MG2008 Discussion Group 1, 22 October 2026: micro/meso/macro sourcing analysis, discussion transcript.

questions.stem: A sourcing team investigates whether withdrawing a contract would leave a town with few alternative livelihoods. Which level is most directly being analysed in the discussion framework?

options.text: Micro: only the retailer’s internal accounting.
Macro: only the wording of national legislation.
No level: wider effects are irrelevant to sourcing.
Meso: the local community.

questions.explanation: Community dependence and alternative local livelihoods are meso considerations. They inform impact assessment without automatically justifying harmful practices.
questions.source: MG2008 Discussion Group 1, 22 October 2026: micro/meso/macro sourcing analysis, discussion transcript.

questions.stem: A buyer checks the applicable national employment rules before judging a supplier’s practices. Which level of the discussion framework is most directly involved?

options.text: Macro: the legal and institutional context.
Micro: the buyer’s personal preference for a brand.
Meso: only the distance between nearby shops.
No level, because all countries necessarily have identical rules.

questions.explanation: The framework places national law and wider institutional context at the macro level. Do not assume the home country’s rules apply unchanged elsewhere.
questions.source: MG2008 Discussion Group 1, 22 October 2026: micro/meso/macro sourcing analysis, discussion transcript.

questions.stem: A buyer worries that some factory workers may be underage. Which initial due-diligence action best matches the discussion?

options.text: Treat the presence of any documents as sufficient without checking reliability.
Verify reliable age and employment records rather than relying on appearance.
Estimate age from appearance and treat the estimate as conclusive.
Assume a low price proves that every worker is underage.

questions.explanation: The practical point is to investigate and verify evidence before deciding. Appearance, prices or unexamined paperwork do not conclusively establish age.
questions.source: MG2008 Discussion Group 1, 22 October 2026: micro/meso/macro sourcing analysis, discussion transcript.

chapters.title: Discussion Group 2: Casas Bahia
chapters.description: Credit inclusion, behavioural marketing and vulnerable-consumer protection.

questions.stem: What underserved need drove Casas Bahia’s model?

options.text: Low-income customers wanted durable goods but lacked conventional credit.
Wealthy customers lacked luxury brands.
Retailers lacked suppliers.
Banks offered unlimited free loans.

questions.explanation: Instalment credit opened access to a large excluded market.

questions.stem: How did recurring in-store repayments support the business?

options.text: They prevented store visits.
They reinforced relationships and created opportunities for further selling.
They removed customer data.
They guaranteed zero default.

questions.explanation: The passbook system combined collection, familiarity and marketing.

questions.stem: What historical monthly interest figure is reported in the case?

options.text: About 4.13%.
About 0.04%.
About 41.3%.
Exactly 8.5%.

questions.explanation: The case reports an average monthly rate of roughly 4.13%.

questions.stem: What historical default rate is reported?

options.text: About 4.13%.
About 30%.
Zero.
About 8.5%.

questions.explanation: The case gives an average default rate of 8.5%.

questions.stem: Why can a low default rate fail to prove customer wellbeing?

options.text: Customers may repay through severe sacrifice or lost essentials.
Default is the only harm.
Repayment guarantees fair pricing.
Wellbeing equals lender return.

questions.explanation: Payment performance does not reveal opportunity cost or distress.

questions.stem: What information is essential for informed instalment credit?

options.text: Only the brand name.
Only the lender’s profit.
Total price, interest, duration, penalties and realistic affordability.
Only the monthly payment.

questions.explanation: Consent requires understanding the full obligation.

questions.stem: How can customer data both help and harm?

options.text: Personalisation always benefits customers.
Privacy applies only to governments.
It can improve tailored credit while enabling manipulation and intrusive profiling.
Data have no ethical effects.

questions.explanation: The same capability can support inclusion or exploitation.

questions.stem: What is the inclusion argument for Casas Bahia?

options.text: It charged no interest.
It avoided behavioural marketing.
It gave excluded consumers access to useful goods and credit histories.
It eliminated all poverty.

questions.explanation: The model opened formal access where banks often did not.

questions.stem: What is the exploitation argument?

options.text: Low-income consumers lack all agency.
Credit cannot create utility.
Affordable-looking instalments and emotional selling may obscure high total cost.
Branded goods are always harmful.

questions.explanation: Vulnerability and information gaps can make consent less informed.

questions.stem: Can the model be both empowering and exploitative?

options.text: No; profit proves exploitation only.
Yes; because ethics is purely relative.
Yes; access can create benefit while design and terms impose unfair pressure.
No; one label must settle every effect.

questions.explanation: Stakeholder effects can be mixed and require evidence on terms and outcomes.

chapters.title: Discussion Group 3: Food Engineering & Industry Science
chapters.description: Industry-funded research, product engineering and unequal responsibility.

questions.stem: Why does industry funding create a structural conflict of interest?

options.text: Academic participation guarantees independence.
Conflicts concern only illegal payments.
Funders may shape questions, governance, interpretation or publication.
Funding proves every result false.

questions.explanation: The risk needs disclosure and safeguards rather than automatic acceptance or dismissal.
questions.source: MG2008 Discussion Group 3; Reading 20; Michael Moss

questions.stem: What would strengthen ILSI research credibility?

options.text: Non-profit branding alone.
Industry-selected questions kept secret.
Suppression of unfavourable results.
Full funding disclosure, independent governance, data access and reproducibility.

questions.stem: What happened at the 1999 food-industry meeting described by Moss?

Consumers set marketing standards.
A collective health response was proposed but rejected amid competitive concerns.
Firms agreed to end sugar use.

questions.explanation: The case illustrates a collective-action problem.
questions.source: MG2008 Discussion Group 3; Reading 20; Michael Moss

questions.stem: What is the bliss point?

options.text: A measure of company profit.
A sensory level, such as sweetness, engineered to maximise liking.
The point where consumers stop eating.
A legal nutrition limit.

questions.explanation: Product testing can optimise sensory appeal.
questions.source: MG2008 Discussion Group 3; Reading 20; Michael Moss

questions.stem: What is sensory-specific satiety?

options.text: A strong repeated flavour becomes less appealing, encouraging the person to stop.
Food melts before swallowing.
A label creates guilt.
Consumers prefer every new flavour.

questions.explanation: Complex flavours may delay this stopping signal.
questions.source: MG2008 Discussion Group 3; Reading 20; Michael Moss

questions.stem: What is vanishing caloric density?

options.text: A food contains no calories.
Calories disappear during sale.
A portion becomes cheaper.
Rapid melting can make the brain underestimate how much is being consumed.

questions.explanation: The sensation can weaken intuitive consumption cues.
questions.source: MG2008 Discussion Group 3; Reading 20; Michael Moss

questions.stem: What ethical concern arises from marketing Lunchables to children’s autonomy?

options.text: Convenience has no benefit.
Shelf life proves healthfulness.
The feeling of control may be used to sell nutritionally weak products to a vulnerable group.
Children never influence purchases.

questions.explanation: Marketing meaning can exploit developmental vulnerability.
questions.source: MG2008 Discussion Group 3; Reading 20; Michael Moss

questions.stem: How can a “healthier” snack label produce moral licensing?

options.text: Reformulation ends marketing.
Health claims are never informative.
Consumers may feel permitted to eat more, offsetting per-serving improvement.
Labels always reduce consumption.

questions.explanation: Total impact depends on behaviour as well as composition.
questions.source: MG2008 Discussion Group 3; Reading 20; Michael Moss

questions.stem: Why was Coca-Cola’s baby-carrot example ethically important?

options.text: The same behavioural tools can promote a healthier product, so context and consequences matter.
Marketing methods are inherently evil.
Carrots and soft drinks are identical.
Transparency is irrelevant.

questions.explanation: Tools are not judged apart from product, audience and likely impact.
questions.source: MG2008 Discussion Group 3; Reading 20; Michael Moss

questions.stem: How should responsibility be divided in engineered-food markets?

options.text: Unequally across consumers, firms and regulators according to knowledge, power and vulnerability.
Consumers alone are responsible.
Firms alone control every choice.
