questions.source: MG2008 Discussion Group 3; Reading 20; Michael Moss

chapters.title: Week 7 — Greener Economies & Wellbeing (Pretty)
chapters.description: Reading-grounded applications of substitution, wellbeing pathways, meaningful attachment and cautious interpretation of historical health costs.

questions.stem: A government concludes from Pretty et al. that additional income never improves wellbeing. What is the best correction?

options.text: Income growth can meet basic needs at low income levels; the link becomes weaker in already affluent settings.
The paper argues that income has exactly the same wellbeing effect at every income level.
The paper claims that only possessions determine wellbeing.
The paper identifies a single income threshold that applies identically to every person.

questions.explanation: The argument distinguishes meeting basic needs from the weaker GDP–wellbeing relationship in affluent populations; it is not a claim that income never matters.
questions.source: MG2008 Reading 10: Pretty et al. (2016), “Improving health and well-being independently of GDP”, original PDF, article pp. 11–30.

questions.stem: A city adds green products to residents’ shopping without reducing other consumption. Why might this fall short of Pretty et al.’s proposal?

options.text: The proposal treats GDP growth as sufficient evidence that all externalities have fallen.
The proposal emphasises substituting sustainable goods and non-material activities for damaging material consumption.
The proposal rejects all purchases, including sustainable goods.
The proposal assumes that an environmental label eliminates the impact of any quantity bought.

questions.explanation: Substitution matters. Efficiency or greener products can be overtaken by growth in total consumption.
questions.source: MG2008 Reading 10: Pretty et al. (2016), “Improving health and well-being independently of GDP”, original PDF, article pp. 11–30.

questions.stem: Which choice best illustrates the paper’s sustainable behaviours involving non-material consumption?

options.text: Replacing every working household device with a new model each year.
Treating higher spending alone as evidence of improved community connections.
Replacing a shopping outing with a community walking and volunteering activity.
Buying additional short-lived products because their advertising uses natural imagery.

questions.explanation: The proposed behaviours include nature contact and community participation, not merely purchasing products presented as green.
questions.source: MG2008 Reading 10: Pretty et al. (2016), “Improving health and well-being independently of GDP”, original PDF, article pp. 11–30.

questions.stem: A neighbourhood walking group improves activity, nature contact and social ties together. How does this fit Pretty et al.’s model?

options.text: Each activity must be assigned to exactly one pathway with no overlaps.
Community ties count only if participants buy products.
Only an increase in GDP can connect these outcomes.
One activity can support several interacting wellbeing pathways.

questions.explanation: The six factors interact. Nature-based social activity can improve several at once, which is also why health-cost categories can overlap.
questions.source: MG2008 Reading 10: Pretty et al. (2016), “Improving health and well-being independently of GDP”, original PDF, article pp. 11–30.

questions.stem: In Pretty et al., what does cathexis help explain about a cherished possession?

options.text: Emotional investment can encourage care and retention rather than rapid disposal and replacement.
Its value depends solely on its current resale price.
It must be replaced frequently to maintain its emotional significance.
Possession attachment is identical to wanting an ever-larger number of goods.

questions.explanation: Cathexis concerns emotional energy invested in an object, activity or place. Meaningful attachment differs from accumulating or continually replacing possessions.
questions.source: MG2008 Reading 10: Pretty et al. (2016), “Improving health and well-being independently of GDP”, original PDF, article pp. 11–30.

questions.stem: A local project builds networks, reciprocity and trust among neighbours. Which asset in Pretty et al.’s framework is most directly being strengthened?

options.text: The turnover rate of disposable goods.
Social capital.
Only physical inventory.
Only financial capital measured by sales revenue.

questions.explanation: The paper treats networks, shared norms, reciprocity and trust as social capital, with potential wellbeing benefits.
questions.source: MG2008 Reading 10: Pretty et al. (2016), “Improving health and well-being independently of GDP”, original PDF, article pp. 11–30.

questions.stem: Why does the paper discuss positive countertrends alongside negative consumption externalities?

options.text: To argue that gardening and volunteering have no possible benefits.
To replace analysis of health effects with product-sales totals.
To recognise beneficial developments without assuming that they have reversed the overall adverse patterns.
To establish that every negative trend is statistically cancelled by one positive trend.

questions.explanation: Examples such as allotments, walking groups and recycling complicate the picture, but the authors do not conclude that all adverse aggregate trends have disappeared.
questions.source: MG2008 Reading 10: Pretty et al. (2016), “Improving health and well-being independently of GDP”, original PDF, article pp. 11–30.

questions.stem: The paper reduces its combined historical health-cost estimate to allow for overlap. What is the methodological reason?

options.text: All costs should be removed whenever a condition has several causes.
A cost reported by the NHS can never also matter to the wider economy.
The adjustment proves that the conditions are statistically independent.
The same person or treatment cost may appear under more than one condition.

questions.explanation: Comorbidity and interactive causes create double-counting risks. The reduction is an assumption to address overlap, not proof of precise causal attribution.
questions.source: MG2008 Reading 10: Pretty et al. (2016), “Improving health and well-being independently of GDP”, original PDF, article pp. 11–30.

questions.stem: How should a student use the paper’s UK health-cost figures in a current Irish policy discussion?

options.text: As historical, context-specific estimates requiring scrutiny, not as current Irish savings guaranteed by an intervention.
As exact current Irish costs because the conditions have the same names.
As proof that every pound of the estimated burden is immediately avoidable.
As a measured return from one nationwide randomised policy trial.

questions.explanation: The paper combines historical UK estimates with assumptions about overlap. Estimated burden is not identical to the achievable savings of a particular policy.
questions.source: MG2008 Reading 10: Pretty et al. (2016), “Improving health and well-being independently of GDP”, original PDF, article pp. 11–30.

questions.stem: Which policy best reflects the paper’s emphasis on prevention and environmental context?

options.text: Require individuals to be active while removing safe walking access.
Create accessible green walking routes and support community activities before ill-health develops.
Wait for illness and treat it without considering living conditions.
Measure wellbeing solely by spending on treatment.

questions.explanation: The authors argue for enabling healthier behaviour through social and environmental conditions, not relying solely on treatment or individual exhortation.
questions.source: MG2008 Reading 10: Pretty et al. (2016), “Improving health and well-being independently of GDP”, original PDF, article pp. 11–30.

chapters.title: Week 7 — Marketing, Consumer Society & Hedonism
chapters.description: Critical reading of the facilitator argument, active consumers, psychological obsolescence and evidence limitations.

questions.stem: Which statement best represents the authors’ conclusion about marketing and consumerism?

options.text: Marketing has no influence on any consumer decision.
Marketing necessarily makes every purchase harmful.
Marketing is more a facilitator than the original manufacturer of consumerism.
Marketing invented material desire in societies that had none.

questions.explanation: The authors reject a single-cause account that treats marketing as the creator of materialism, while acknowledging its influence and costs.
questions.source: MG2008 Reading 11: O’Shaughnessy and O’Shaughnessy, “Marketing, the consumer society and hedonism”, original PDF, especially printed pp. 525, 543–545.

questions.stem: A critic describes advertising as injecting desires into passive consumers. What response most closely matches the reading?

options.text: Consumers always resist all advertising successfully.
Every purchase is a reflex with no interpretation.
Only marketers can attach meanings to products.
Consumers can filter, interpret and negotiate marketing meanings rather than simply absorb them.

questions.explanation: The authors favour a more active, negotiated account over a simple hypodermic stimulus–response model. This does not imply zero marketing influence.
questions.source: MG2008 Reading 11: O’Shaughnessy and O’Shaughnessy, “Marketing, the consumer society and hedonism”, original PDF, especially printed pp. 525, 543–545.

questions.stem: Why would equating marketing solely with advertising weaken an analysis of the reading?

options.text: Marketing also includes identifying segments, shaping offerings and making them available.
Advertising is unrelated to marketing in every circumstance.
The reading defines marketing solely as setting factory wages.
The reading argues that distribution choices never affect consumers.

questions.explanation: The account includes market selection, product offerings, availability and communication, among other decisions; promotion is only part of it.
questions.source: MG2008 Reading 11: O’Shaughnessy and O’Shaughnessy, “Marketing, the consumer society and hedonism”, original PDF, especially printed pp. 525, 543–545.

questions.stem: A working phone is discarded because promotion makes the newer model seem socially necessary. Which criticism does the reading acknowledge?

options.text: Material possessions cannot carry social meanings.
Psychological obsolescence can encourage replacement of serviceable products.
Functional breakdown is the only possible cause of replacement.
Every new model necessarily reduces waste.

questions.explanation: The authors acknowledge waste and the role of marketing in celebrating newer models, even while disputing that marketing created consumerism.
questions.source: MG2008 Reading 11: O’Shaughnessy and O’Shaughnessy, “Marketing, the consumer society and hedonism”, original PDF, especially printed pp. 525, 543–545.

questions.stem: An effective campaign discourages smoking. How does this example function in the authors’ argument?

options.text: Health campaigns prove that commercial promotion has no costs.
A beneficial campaign means audiences have no agency.
Marketing techniques can also be used to oppose consumption habits.
Any campaign using persuasion must increase total smoking.

questions.explanation: The reading treats marketing as a set of techniques that can serve different purposes, including reducing consumption, rather than as inherently consumption-increasing.
questions.source: MG2008 Reading 11: O’Shaughnessy and O’Shaughnessy, “Marketing, the consumer society and hedonism”, original PDF, especially printed pp. 525, 543–545.

questions.stem: What qualification do the authors make about the evidential strength of their paper?

options.text: They report a controlled experiment proving advertising never changes behaviour.
They calculate an exact share of consumerism caused by each advertisement.
They claim the concepts are straightforward to measure without empirical inquiry.
They acknowledge the absence of relevant data and the difficulty of measuring key concepts.

questions.explanation: The conclusion identifies a lack of relevant data and measurement challenges. The argument should not be presented as decisive experimental proof.
questions.source: MG2008 Reading 11: O’Shaughnessy and O’Shaughnessy, “Marketing, the consumer society and hedonism”, original PDF, especially printed pp. 525, 543–545.

questions.stem: A student argues that because materialism existed before modern advertising, advertising cannot intensify it. What is the best evaluation?

options.text: Earlier materialism challenges a claim that advertising invented it, but does not rule out later influence.
Historical precedence proves that advertising has no effect.
Materialism’s earlier existence proves modern advertising caused that earlier materialism.
The timing of materialism is irrelevant to a claim about its invention.

questions.explanation: Distinguish origin from reinforcement. The authors’ facilitator argument is compatible with acknowledging influence and psychological obsolescence.
questions.source: MG2008 Reading 11: O’Shaughnessy and O’Shaughnessy, “Marketing, the consumer society and hedonism”, original PDF, especially printed pp. 525, 543–545.

questions.stem: Which paired interpretation best compares Pretty et al. with the marketing reading?

options.text: Both papers use the same experiment to show that income never matters.
Pretty et al. examine consumption’s wellbeing costs and alternatives; the marketing authors challenge a simple account blaming marketing for originating consumerism.
Both papers establish that marketing alone explains all health problems.
Pretty et al. reject all benefits of material consumption, while the marketing authors reject all costs.

questions.explanation: The texts address related issues from different angles. Neither requires denying all benefits or all costs of consumption.
questions.source: MG2008 Reading 11: O’Shaughnessy and O’Shaughnessy, “Marketing, the consumer society and hedonism”, original PDF, especially printed pp. 525, 543–545.

chapters.title: Week 7 — TOMS, Aid Effectiveness & Recipient Agency
chapters.description: Separate charitable intent and output from outcomes, cost-effectiveness, comparative evidence and recipient agency.

questions.stem: A company cites the number of shoes donated as proof that children’s educational outcomes improved. Which distinction is missing?

options.text: Higher shoe sales automatically measure school attendance.
An outcome is simply another name for the quantity distributed.
An output delivered is not the same as an outcome achieved.
Donations cannot be counted under any circumstances.

questions.explanation: Counting shoes establishes an activity or output. Educational benefit requires evidence about outcomes such as attendance.
questions.source: MG2008 Reading 12: Amanda Taub (2015), “Buying TOMS shoes is a terrible way to help poor people”, and appended Wydick commentary, original supplied DOCX.

questions.stem: Which statement accurately reflects the shoe-donation findings reported in the TOMS reading?

options.text: Every measured outcome improved dramatically.
No child used or valued the shoes.
The study proved that shoe donations destroyed every local business.
Children liked and used the shoes, but no significant improvement in school attendance or self-esteem was found.

questions.explanation: The account distinguishes some use and enjoyment from the absence of significant improvements on the highlighted wider outcomes.
questions.source: MG2008 Reading 12: Amanda Taub (2015), “Buying TOMS shoes is a terrible way to help poor people”, and appended Wydick commentary, original supplied DOCX.

questions.stem: What is the key untested assumption when a campaign claims that giving girls a particular consumer item will resolve school absence?

options.text: That lack of the item is the decisive barrier, rather than other constraints such as facilities or pain.
That schools and families can have any influence on attendance.
That the item can be physically distributed.
That all charitable activity must be commercial.

questions.explanation: The reading warns against jumping from an observed hardship to a presumed single material cause and solution.
questions.source: MG2008 Reading 12: Amanda Taub (2015), “Buying TOMS shoes is a terrible way to help poor people”, and appended Wydick commentary, original supplied DOCX.

questions.stem: Why does the TOMS reading propose considering cash transfers as a comparator?

options.text: Recipient choice is irrelevant once donors have good intentions.
Recipients may have information about their own priorities that an outside donor lacks.
Cash is proven superior to every good or service in every context.
The original TOMS evaluation randomly compared shoes with cash and settled the question.

questions.explanation: Cash can allow recipients to choose among needs. The reading explicitly says TOMS had not run a comparable cash-versus-own-programme study and does not claim cash always wins.
questions.source: MG2008 Reading 12: Amanda Taub (2015), “Buying TOMS shoes is a terrible way to help poor people”, and appended Wydick commentary, original supplied DOCX.

questions.stem: A campaign depicts recipients as helpless people awaiting rescue by shoppers. What ethical concern is most directly raised?

options.text: It proves that the product cannot be sold at a profit.
It means no buyer can have genuinely charitable motives.
It can diminish recipient agency and reinforce a paternalistic view of poverty.
It gives recipients too much control over the programme design.

questions.explanation: The critique targets a donor-centred story that sidelines recipients’ knowledge and agency, not a claim that all buyers have bad intentions.
questions.source: MG2008 Reading 12: Amanda Taub (2015), “Buying TOMS shoes is a terrible way to help poor people”, and appended Wydick commentary, original supplied DOCX.

questions.stem: How does the appended commentary qualify the strongest criticism of TOMS’ effects on local shoe markets?

options.text: It proves every local shoe vendor permanently closed.
It reports that market effects were never considered.
It establishes that all imported donations increase local sales.
It describes a small negative effect, not wholesale destruction of local markets.

questions.explanation: The commentary reports some displacement of local sales but characterises the effect as small. Avoid turning that into an unsupported claim of destroyed markets.
questions.source: MG2008 Reading 12: Amanda Taub (2015), “Buying TOMS shoes is a terrible way to help poor people”, and appended Wydick commentary, original supplied DOCX.

questions.stem: Which organisational response in the appended TOMS commentary is most consistent with evidence-based responsibility?

options.text: Commission evaluation, disclose findings and adapt the intervention to recipients’ needs.
Treat good intentions as sufficient reason to avoid evaluation.
Suppress disappointing findings to preserve the campaign’s image.
Count only sales growth when assessing recipient wellbeing.

questions.explanation: The appended researcher praises transparency, willingness to evaluate and changes in shoe type and programme design. The case is not a uniformly negative judgement of the organisation.
questions.source: MG2008 Reading 12: Amanda Taub (2015), “Buying TOMS shoes is a terrible way to help poor people”, and appended Wydick commentary, original supplied DOCX.

questions.stem: Why might directly providing a good still be justified in some contexts, according to the TOMS reading?

options.text: A community benefit guarantees that any chosen product is cost-effective.
Some interventions, such as vaccinations, can generate benefits beyond the individual recipient.
Cash has been shown to fail in every poverty programme.
Donors always know more about every need than recipients.

questions.explanation: The reading gives community-wide benefits as one reason direct provision might make sense. It still calls for comparison and evidence, not a blanket rule.
questions.source: MG2008 Reading 12: Amanda Taub (2015), “Buying TOMS shoes is a terrible way to help poor people”, and appended Wydick commentary, original supplied DOCX.
